narrationScript: Beyond theoretical complexities, it's vital to consider practical implications. A common mistake is assuming simple algorithms are always 'good enough.' While O(n^2) algorithms like these might be acceptable for very small datasets, say less than 50 elements, their performance degrades astronomically as 'n' grows. For example, sorting a million items with an O(n^2) algorithm would involve a trillion operations, making it practically unusable. In contrast, more advanced O(n log n) algorithms would only take tens of millions of operations. All three algorithms we discussed are 'in-place,' meaning they sort elements within the original array without needing significant extra memory. They also differ in 'stability.' A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements. Bubble Sort and Insertion Sort can be implemented stably, which is important in some applications, while Selection Sort is generally not stable. Always consider your data size and specific requirements when choosing a sorting method.
